opening.prompt: Is this your first time taking the Set for Life Financial Assessment?

options.label: Yes
No

opening.prompt: Before we get started, how “Set for Life” do you feel financially right now?

A little
Somewhat
Mostly

questions.prompt: If someone asked you to describe your financial picture today—not every penny, but the big picture—how clearly could you do it?

I know pieces of it, but there are significant gaps.
I have a general idea, but I would need to look some things up.
I have a pretty clear picture.

questions.prompt: Thinking about the environment you grew up in, which statements best describe your experience with money?

options.label: Money was talked about openly, and I learned quite a bit by being included.
I picked up some useful money lessons, but there were also things I had to figure out for myself.
Money was mostly handled privately, so I learned more by watching than by being taught directly.
Money conversations usually happened when there was a problem, concern, or need.
I received mixed or conflicting messages about money.
Money wasn't discussed very much at all.
My experience doesn't fit neatly into these choices.

questions.prompt: Thinking about the past six months, how often have you felt like there was more month left than money available to handle it?

options.label: Almost every month
Many months
Some months
Rarely

questions.prompt: How clearly can you describe what you want your money to make possible over the next several years?

options.label: I haven't really defined that yet.
I have ideas, but they're pretty general.
I can name a few things I want financially.
I have a fairly clear picture of what I'm working toward.
I can clearly describe the life or outcomes I want my money to help make possible.

questions.prompt: By the end of a typical month, how well do you understand where your money went?

options.label: I often wonder where it went.
I can account for the major bills, but a meaningful amount is hard to explain.
I generally know where it went, although some spending gets away from me.
I have a clear sense of where most of it went.
I can clearly identify the major patterns in where my money went.

questions.prompt: Today, when money needs to be discussed honestly, how comfortable are you having that conversation?

options.label: Very uncomfortable — I would rather avoid it.
Somewhat uncomfortable — I can do it, but I don't like it.
I can talk about money when necessary, but there are some things I'd rather keep to myself.
Fairly comfortable — I can usually talk about it when the conversation is useful.
Very comfortable — I can discuss money openly when there's a reason to.

questions.prompt: Think about an unexpected expense that would be noticeable for your household but not financially catastrophic. When something like that comes up, what usually happens?

options.label: It throws my finances significantly off track.
I usually have to delay something else, borrow, or carry the expense forward.
I can manage it, but it creates noticeable financial pressure.
I can usually handle it with a temporary adjustment.

questions.prompt: When you hear different financial advice from social media, videos, podcasts, family, friends, books, or professionals, what usually happens?

options.label: I often feel overwhelmed and don't know where to start.
The conflicting advice sometimes makes me put off making decisions.
I listen to different viewpoints but sometimes struggle to determine what applies to me.
I can usually sort through the information and identify what deserves more investigation.
I have a process for separating useful information from information that doesn't apply to my situation.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes how most of your financial decisions get made?

options.label: Whatever needs attention first usually gets the money.
I mostly respond to bills, needs, and situations as they come up.
I try to plan, but immediate needs often change the plan.
Most of my money decisions are intentional, even when I have to adjust.
I generally decide what my money needs to accomplish before competing demands decide for me.

questions.prompt: How much have you intentionally examined the money beliefs you picked up along the way?

options.label: I haven't really thought about where my money beliefs came from.
I've noticed some of them, but haven't examined them very deeply.
I've questioned some beliefs while continuing to follow others.
I've intentionally examined many of my beliefs and changed some of them.
I regularly question whether my financial beliefs still fit the life I'm trying to build.

questions.prompt: After your regular bills and necessary expenses are handled, how much money is typically left for things like saving, paying extra toward debt, preparing for future needs, enjoying life, or handling something unexpected?

options.label: None or almost none
Very little
Some, but I have to make careful choices about where it goes
A reasonable amount
Enough that I usually have room to address several priorities

questions.prompt: When two seemingly credible sources give different financial advice, how confident are you deciding what deserves further consideration?

options.label: Not confident — I wouldn't really know how to evaluate them.
Slightly confident — I might go with whichever sounds more convincing.
Somewhat confident — I would research more, but I can still get stuck.
Confident — I know what questions to ask and what information I need.
Very confident — I can evaluate the reasoning, determine what applies to my situation, and seek additional expertise when needed.

questions.prompt: How much have you thought through what would happen financially if your household experienced a major disruption?

options.label: I mostly deal with those things if and when they happen.
I've thought about them, but I don't really know how my finances would respond.
I've considered some risks but not others.
I've intentionally thought through several of the major risks that could affect me.

questions.prompt: If sharing some financial information could help you get useful guidance, how comfortable would you be sharing what's necessary with someone you trust?

options.label: I'd still prefer not to share it.
I'd share only very limited information.
It would depend on what they needed and why.
I'd share what's necessary once I understood why it mattered.

questions.prompt: After your regular bills and necessary expenses are accounted for, which statement best describes what happens with any money that's available?

I make some intentional decisions about it, but not consistently.

questions.prompt: Think about the financial information you've learned over the past year. Which statement best describes what usually happens next?

options.label: I consume a lot of information, but very little changes afterward.
I often learn something useful but don't know what to do with it.
I understand more than I act on.
I usually identify an appropriate next step when something applies to me.

questions.prompt: Suppose something changes and you need to free up money for a new priority. Which statement sounds most like you?

options.label: I wouldn't really know where the money could come from.

questions.prompt: A financial professional explains a recommendation, but there's a part you don't fully understand. What are you most likely to do?

options.label: Assume they know more about this than I do and move forward based on their recommendation.
Ask a quick question, but probably rely mostly on their judgment.
Take some time before deciding, even if I'm not sure what else I need to know.

demographics._placement: Demographics/Profile step, alongside D1-D3. NOT the front door, NOT a Money Moment, NOT the Snapshot cover, and nothing that implies it affects the Money Picture.
demographics._note: The jurisdiction options come from the controlled `jurisdictions` table via lib/profile/jurisdiction.ts rather than being duplicated here, so the selector, the API validation and the DB constraint cannot drift. 'Prefer not to say' is an EXPLICIT option, matching D1-D3, so a decline is a recorded choice rather than an absent value.

spec_notes: OPEN JUDGEMENT CALL: task brief asked for internal_id values like OPENING_A, but the spec S10 literally heads the items OPEN_A / OPEN_B with option codes OPEN_A_A / OPEN_B_A. Used OPEN_A and OPEN_B as internal_id (matching the spec's own codes) with section_label Opening A / Opening B. No wording affected.

ACTIVATION TYPE INFERENCE: spec S11 gives no explicit Type/Required lines for A1-A4 (unlike S9/S10). Treated all four as required single_select because S8 counts A1-A4 in the 31 required responses and S17 stores each separately. Flagging for spec owner to confirm rather than altering wording.
OPEN-TEXT BLANKS: Q21_H, Q9_M, Q16_K and D2_C carry a write-in blank rendered in the spec as ________. Preserved verbatim in the label and added an open_text:true structural flag; no wording changed.

EM-DASH / CURLY-QUOTE FIDELITY: prompts and labels preserve the spec's em dashes (Q2, Q4, Q16_F, Q18, Q24, activation A4) and the curly double quotes around “Set for Life” (OPEN_B, Q16 prompt, Q16_J) exactly as printed. ONE DEVIATION WAS FOUND AND FIXED: Q16_J originally carried U+2019 RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK where the spec has U+0027 APOSTROPHE. The spec uses U+0027 exclusively across the question sections (69 occurrences, zero U+2019), so that was genuine drift, not a typographic variant. It is now byte-exact. An earlier version of this note claimed “nothing normalized”, which that drift falsified — the claim was wrong and is corrected here. tests/unit/wording-fidelity.test.ts now compares raw code points and fails on any difference, so this class of drift cannot recur silently.

SCORING BEHAVIOR PROSE: recorded verbatim behavior keys from S9 (profile_1_5, classifier, capacity_override_first_else_2_5, capacity_override_last_else_1_5, profile_1_5_with_capacity_modifier). No thresholds invented; scoring config is a separate file.

DEMOGRAPHICS REQUIRED FLAG: D1-D3 marked required:false / required_for_completion:false because S8 separates demographics from diagnostic completion; Prefer not to say is a valid completed demographic response per S6/S8 and never a diagnostic signal. UI still presents all three.

DEMOGRAPHICS TYPE INFERENCE: spec S12 gives no explicit Type/Required lines for D1-D3 (unlike S9/S10). Treated as single_select because each is a single-choice list. This is an AUTHOR INFERENCE, not spec text — flagged for spec-owner confirmation, exactly as the A1-A4 type inference above is. The required:false / required_for_completion:false flags ARE grounded in S8 (demographics are separate from diagnostic completion).
